payload.theorem_nl: Let $p$ be a prime number greater than $3$. For each $k \\in \\{1,\\dots,p-1\\}$, let $I(k) \\in \\{1,2,\\dots,p-1\\}$ be such that $k \\cdot I(k) \\equiv 1 \\pmod{p}$. Prove that the number of integers $k \\in \\{1,\\dots,p-2\\}$ such that $I(k+1) < I(k)$ is greater than $p/4-1$.

assembly_plan.proof_skeleton_nl: Fix a prime p>3 and define I_p and S_p exactly as in the theorem. First separate the boundary case p=5; L7 proves the theorem there directly. Now assume p>5. By L2, the descent set is symmetric under reflection k -> p-1-k, so the left and right halves contain equally many descents. By L3, the middle index (p-1)/2 is always a descent. The genuinely new ingredient, replacing the invalid covering argument from the rejected attempts, is L6: it gives a quantitative lower bound on the number of descents already present in the left half. Doubling that lower bound using the symmetry from L2 and then adding the forced middle descent from L3 yields |S_p| >= 2*((p-3)/8)+1. Finally apply the elementary inequality in L8 to conclude |S_p| > p/4 - 1. Combining this with the base case p=5 yields the exact root theorem.

steps.derives: If p=5, then the theorem holds: with S_5 = { k in {1,2,3} : I_5(k+1)<I_5(k) }, one has |S_5| > 5/4 - 1.
steps.trivial_justification: This is exactly the content of L7.

steps.derives: For the rest of the proof, it remains to treat the case p>5.
steps.trivial_justification: The theorem only concerns primes p>3, so after handling p=5 separately it is enough to assume p>5.

steps.derives: With S_p = { k in {1,...,p-2} : I_p(k+1)<I_p(k) }, the reflection map r(k)=p-1-k preserves S_p. In particular, the number of elements of S_p in the left half {1,...,(p-3)/2} equals the number of elements of S_p in the right half {(p+1)/2,...,p-2}.
steps.trivial_justification: L2 gives the equivalence k in S_p iff p-1-k in S_p for each k in {1,...,p-2}. Since p>5 is odd, the map k |-> p-1-k is a bijection from {1,...,(p-3)/2} onto {(p+1)/2,...,p-2}. Therefore the two halves contribute equally many descents.

steps.derives: The central index (p-1)/2 belongs to S_p.
steps.trivial_justification: This is exactly the final conclusion of L3.
This is exactly the statement of L6.

By A3, the right half of S_p has the same cardinality as the left half, so the two outer halves together contribute at least 2*|(S_p ∩ {1,...,(p-3)/2})|. By A5 this is at least 2*((p-3)/8). By A4 the central index (p-1)/2 is also in S_p, and it is disjoint from the two halves. Adding that central element yields |S_p| >= 2*((p-3)/8)+1.
A6 gives |S_p| >= 2*((p-3)/8)+1. L8 states that 2*((p-3)/8)+1 > p/4 - 1 for every prime p>5. Hence |S_p| > p/4 - 1.

steps.derives: For every prime p>3, if I_p(k) is the unique inverse of k modulo p and S_p = { k in {1,...,p-2} : I_p(k+1) < I_p(k) }, then |S_p| > p/4 - 1.
steps.trivial_justification: The theorem is proved by cases. If p=5, A1 gives the claim. If p>5, A7 gives the claim. These are the only possibilities for a prime p>3.

candidates.strategy_summary: Use three arithmetic structural facts about the modular-inverse permutation that were missing from the rejected attempts: reflection symmetry of descents, a forced central descent at k=(p-1)/2, and a genuine half-range lower bound on descents in the left half of the index set. This differs from the failed interval-covering strategy by not trying to deduce the theorem from the weak statement 'every 4-block contains a descent' alone; instead it adds a stronger arithmetic counting input and handles the boundary case p=5 separately.
